Emergency Services Shortage Crisis

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
When you dial 10111 in a medical emergency you rely on proficient care on the spot. New regulation on EMS personnel qualifications threatens to put your life, and their livelihoods on the line.

Unique Selling Point:
In January 2017 the Health Professionals council of South Africa and the Department of health introduced a new regulation that revokes recognition of the six-week basic life support, six-month intermediate life support and nine-month advanced life support courses for paramedics, that have been serving the industry up till now. A basic life support paramedic now has to complete a two-year course, and those wanting to become advanced life support paramedics must do a four-year degree. This could put the entire industry in jeopardy as well as put our live's in danger.

Summary:
The new regulation has evoked concern amongst EMS practitioners and private Emergency service providers as well as private training academies, that it will limit progress for individuals already in the system with six weeks basic or even intermediary life support qualifications, as this means that in order to now get higher qualifications they would quit their jobs in order to attend a mandatory full time course for three years or more to get more qualified in the field.

Paul Masita, a 50 year old Intermediary Paramedic fears his career advancement is over, he has a family and two children to support and full time study would be out of the question.

The colleges currently running the short courses will have to close those programmes down and there is no light coming for accreditation from the HPCSA and SAQA. With only four universities currently running with the courses how are we going to get enough paramedic's into the field?

The Department of Health is adamant that they want to professionalise the industry even if there is some collateral damage along the way. They assert that many of these colleges are cash cows, churning out basic paramedic's who may never find a job. In the mean time we may not have services that can effectively save lives or even worse they could end up costing the average citizen a lot more. Paramedic's with degrees are far more expensive to hire.

A group of concerned Emergency Services providers and organizations are not taking this lying down and are planning on taking the Department of Health to court later this month. Carte Blanche investigates.

Further information:
There are about 140 000 registered basic life support paramedics on the HPCSA register and only about 18 thousand of them are employed. South Africa already has a shortage of intermediate and advance life support paramedics, even with the current system of short courses qualifications.

In 2008 South Africa had 1631 registered advanced life support (ALS) paramedics to provide pre-hospital advanced life support care to a population of approximately 50 million. Compared to globally accepted ratios, the number of ALS paramedics in South Africa can be considered as grossly inadequate.

The reasoning behind this regulation is that is that the profession needs to be recognized within the current educational framework and the current short courses do not provide that. The regulation will also eliminate bogus colleges that have used the system as a cash cow while producing unskilled paramedics into the system. However the short courses academies has been a reliable system for the health industry until now producing over 60 basic life support paramedics every 6 weeks who would then work their way to becoming Advance life support practitioners within a short time of two to three years. From 2018 onwards the HPCSA will effectively close its register only recognizing a university qualification from a two-year basic life support course to a four-year Advance life support qualification.


There are currently only four universities offering the course, being the University of Johannesburg, University of the western cape, Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University and the Durban University of technology. According to Oliver Wright, CEO of South African Ambulance emergency services association, besides the fact that university education is inaccessible and expensive for many South Africans with poor financial background, the course will now only be offered in four provinces making it hard for ordinary citizens to acquire the qualification.

The Paramedics industry is also hard hit by an exodus of skilled professionals leaving the country every year to work in countries where they get paid over R100 000 tax free monthly as compared to the 20 to 30 000 they would get here as advanced life support medics. To add to that there is also professionals that retire every year, so with all that, it will be very difficult to replace these skilled workers with only four universities producing about 60 graduates annually that have very little practical experience.

Christiaan, a director at the De Vries academy in Pretoria one of the largest EMS academies in the country also made mention that with the fact that they will now be required to shut down their operations, this adds to the long queue of unemployment for many people across the country which in recent weeks has been said to be at it’s most highest since 2003. Cris says the De Vries academy and other associations are currently in the process of taking the Department of Health to the court of law to have this new regulation reviewed. They hope for the filing process complete by June.

Generally it is believed that the regulation is good for the EMS industry but the concern is the fact that the government is quick to shut down the short courses without outlining a clear plan to curb the low number of Intermediate and Advance life support professionals that are to be produced by the University. The government sector is already the hardest hit in this shortage compared to the private sector and it is a national problem primarily in rural arrears of the country. Does this mean that dying South Africans might soon be in trouble due to a lack of enough skilled professionals on at an emergency scene? Carte Blanche investigates.

We speak first to Neil Gargan, chairman of South African Ambulance emergency services association as he shares with us his concerns. Oliver will also highlight the shocking statistics of how many qualified paramedics are employed in the country as well and his view in terms of where he feels the shortage will come from as well as his journey with the HPCSA and the Department of health when he tried to address his concern with them.

Case study- Paul Masita is a 50-year-old paramedic who has been on the job for over 15 years. He has an Intermediate life support qualification acquired through the short courses. Paul is a family man and is hoping to study further to get a an Advanced life support qualification but with the new regulation he fears he can’t achieve that as he does not have the luxury to quit his job and go to university full time.

Chris, Manager at De Vries academy tells us how long their academy has been running from and how many skilled paramedics have they produced. He also shares with us how shutting their academy doors will affect them both from a point of employment as well practitioners in the Emergency services. Along with other academies and associations, they plan to take The Department of Health and the HPCSA to court before end of June 2017.

David Stanton from NetCare 911 sees the regulation as a good thing and something that will have the industry in a good place in the next 20 years. According to Dave this is not something that’s unique to South Africa but he does agree that there might be a learning gap created that the government hasn’t really addressed as far as the paramedics in the current system are concerned.

Case Study- Tegan Gudlloud is a 26-year-old passionate paramedic. She has an intermediate Life support qualification that has already cost her over R90000 in fees. She has a desire to study further and become and Advanced life support paramedic. Tegan’s challenge now is that if she is to study further she will have to quit her job and attend varsity full time. She feels this will put her under financial strain and that quitting her job is not an option that will suit her.

Mr Raveen Naidoo, Director of EMS at the NDH says the regulation will work. When is it supposed to take effect? According to him there is a plan to curb the anticipated further decline in the number of graduates produced annually. Raveen believes the new regulation has been in the pipeline for a while and that the private training academies knew about it and their concerns are only from a commercial point of view.

Willie Lightfoot is the CEO of LifeMed Private Ambulance services. Willie says the new regulation will hamper them as business people because they will not be willing to pay someone for the duration of them attending a full time cause. The financial implications of having to pay higher salaries to the university qualified people who will be doing the same jobs as the short current ones is also a an issue Willie is opposed to.

HPCSA, on the regulation and how they think it will impact the industry and what measures are they putting in place to fill the gap when there is a shortage of EMS professionals in the field, and what are they going to do to ensure that the current paramedics' advancement is not hampered by this new regulation. How are they going to ensure that the public is not jeopardised when critical medical care is in short supply?

Ultimately the Government’s regulation is believed to be a good initiative in the long run, however the impact that it will have on the many paramedics and the private businesses in the industry seems to be an oversight on their part. How this new regulation affect the normal south African in the streets in times of emergency in the future and will the industry itself take a knock as private ambulance agencies are forced to shutdown? Carte Blanche investigates.

Press Release:


New government regulations doing away with short courses for Emergency Medical Care practitioners could result in a critical shortage of advanced life support paramedics.Emergency Medical Services in Crisis
When your life is on the line, you call emergency medical services and hope for proficient, skilled care on the spot. In 80% of emergencies, patients rely on the care of basic
life support practitioners, who have generally qualified through 4-week short courses, which government says are not up to the professional standards required. But new
regulations will signal the end of short courses and EMS practitioners will be forced to complete formal degrees of up to 4 years. This has sparked fears that it will result in
an even bigger shortage of advanced life-support practitioners. Carte Blanche investigates

Script:


Dispatch: Private Ambulance services do you have an emergency?…. My wife has been shot. She is dying please


VO: Violent Crimes and High accident road deaths make South Africa one of the most perilous countries in the world. With over 14000 road fatalities reported in 2016, we often rely on emergency care givers to be our life savers.

Tegan: if I don't get up in the morning and come to work and help someone that person is going to die
so the reason I do it is to [00:08:19.10] give someone an extra day

VO: Tegan Genlloud is one of the many dedicated emergency care givers with over 6 years experience.

Dispatch: The Ambulance is 3 minutes away. Is your wife still breathing?

LINK: On the HPCSA register there are around,
55 000 emergency care personnel with only a 4 week basic life support qualification. Around 18 000 of them are employed by industry while the rest are unemployed or worse, under skilled.
So are we really receiving the best care there is?

Beat// person screaming on side of the stretcher

VO: This privately filmed footage by an emergency care giver was sent to Carte Blanche. At this accident scene two basic life support medics are attending to some of the injured. We can clearly see that they have omitted to treat a severely injured person, then proceed to load him into the ambulance through the side door - dropping the patient in the process.

This kind of malpractice is not uncommon according to John, a highly experienced advanced life support paramedic. His identity is protected for fear of being targeted by other industry players.

Jon: The quality in all honesty is shocking. They have a certificate that says that they are competent in various skills, yet when they come to work they are unable to perform any of those basic skills. They won't even know if a patient has a pulse or doesn't have a pulse.

VO: At this accident scene - Basic life support crews are clearly violating the medical code of ethics, loading 10 injured patients into one Ambulance, then making some of them sit on the front seat without even treating them.

John: there are lot of these small little fringe private services popping up, but there is no proper regulation. They don't have the basic equipment that's needed for the patient. . They will put 11 or 12 patients in an ambulance to go and claim against the road accident fund.

LINK: Rogue elements appear to have emerged within the emergency medical services industry, tarnishing the profession. In addition dishonest private colleges have mushroomed around the country offering short courses, churning out Basic Ambulance assistants by the thousands.

John: People have these high hopes they can go and do a four week course, pay anything from 8 to 15,16 thousand rand for their four week course, they do the course, thinking they're going to be a paramedic but they're not a paramedic they're a medic.

And now that they have this qualification they believe they can get employment and it doesn't happen.

VO: After qualifying, desperate basic ambulance assistants can find themselves jobless and penniless, Zodwa Sibanyoni is one such victim

Zodwa:I quit my job to go and study to be a paramedic as it was a passion of mine.

VO: She qualified 3 years ago as a Basic Ambulance Assistant and paid R11 500 for her course.

Zodwa: They just tell you that it is a jungle out there. They don’t tell you that there a lot of you out there and you might not get a job.

Zodwa: I tend to suffer from depression at times My health has deteriorated as a result


VO: Although there are many credible institutions producing competent medics, John knows of some that are unscrupulous.

John: There was some college in Limpopo where some people were coming on a Friday and on Saturday would fetch their certificate and then when they're employed what happens is, they cant even take a blood pressure

LINK: In January this year the department of health introduced a new regulation that no longer recognizes the short course training for all emergency medical services.

VO: Lesiba Malotana of the HPCSA says the short courses do not help to professionalise the emergency care industry, especially with so many jobless.

Lesiba : Thats correct they're no longer going to produce more and the rationale is that there is enough. and if they’re not able to find employment is there a need to continue producing? Is that not perpetrating unemployment even poverty

Zodwa: The government posts are only advertised once a year. I haven’t even seen any in a while. I keep applying but nothing happens. 75% of the people I went to class with we’re all unemployed.

Lesiba: the short courses are just skills based while if you want to produce a competent wholesome practitioner. why should an entry level paramedic not end up with a PhD in emergency care

VO: By the end of this year the 4 week Basic life support course will be discontinued and replaced with a full time one year Higher certificate. The 4 month Intermediate course will be stopped by 2019, replaced with a 2 year diploma and the 9 month Advance Life support course also ends by 2019, replaced with a 4 year degree.

VO: Willie Lightfoot an ambulance service provider and veteran paramedic, says these changes are going to lead to a crisis.

Willie: its not going to be enough personnel that can man the ambulance, especially on advanced life support.

VO: Advanced life Support practitioners are already in short supply, they're a scarce skill and easily poached internationally.

Willie: the one big problem that we see is the ICU transfers, in other words the guys that really are critical, babies that are choking, people that stopped breathing, there is not going to be enough advanced life support paramedics, because it now takes 4 years to get an advanced qualified paramedics on the new system

VO: Tegan is an intermediate life support medic, and has first hand experience on how a shortage of advanced life support paramedics plays out in an emergency situation.

Tegan: they will dispatch an ambulance out first and then the ambulance will assess the situation and if we need further equipment or drugs or anything that is in the advanced scope of practice we will phone for that vehicle to come out and assist us the likelihood of getting a paramedic on one of the ambulances is minimal

John: if there are 70 life support paramedics in Gauteng and you are sending 50 of them on a 4 year course, where are you going to get the other 50 to replace them?

VO: At present there are only 4 universities offering the four year degree, and a fifth one coming on board soon. They will produce about 60 to 100 B-Tech graduates per year, who will eventually replace the current Advanced Life Support paramedics but that won't be enough to feed into the system, says Christiaan Visser, from the emergency medical care training association.

Christiaan: Nobody is fighting against upgrading the short courses, nobody is saying that we shouldn't have tertiary education,. What we are saying is who's going to fill up the gap between short course trained people and tertiary education.

If you look at the staff turn over in the ambulance industry it is much higher than that amount that the universities are able to produce

VO: It also means that current medics who want to advance their short course qualification will have to go into full time study. Tegan has already spent 94 000 rand on her courses and is still paying back the debt

Tegan: for me there is no way forward with my expenses I cant take 2 years off of work or 4 years off of work and go and study that higher qualification,

John: The problem is would your company pay for you to take 5 years off work or 4 years off work to go and study full time at university and they employ another paramedic in your place so they're paying dual salary...My company won't do that

Willie: they would rather downgrade the current critical care paramedics like us to a lower level so we cant do the skill, so we did it yesterday if they change the law I cant help you with my medicine, I cant give it anymore

Link: The HPCSA is the body that sets the scope for the curriculum for all emergency medical care staff. They admit that the curriculum is below par.

Lesiba : i think one of the biggest things we must never do is pretend these people have not been the backbone of health system Unfortunately, the difficulties is when the course was so badly designed that is cant be repackaged to be able to articulate into something

LINK: Discussions have been going on since 2003 to upgrade the qualification but stakeholders say that the voice of the industry is falling on deaf ears

Christiaan: We've written many letters to the health profession council asking do you understand the implication of closing the short courses, do you understand whats going to happen to the industry and the public?
John: We know nothing, we haven't received any information - everything is done behind closed doors and we only know through it leaking out .In 15 years i've had one newsletter posted to me

VO: As part of the fallout many of the colleges offering short courses will have to close down. Accreditation is a long and costly process.

Christiaan: At the moment there are around 30 private education and training providers who will have to close their doors so we're looking at 2000 job losses

John: I personally am all for them stopping the basic ambulance courses, it's a quick money making scheme that even four weeks you're turning over millions and there's been no proper regulation

Zodwa: I regret doing the course, I regret being a paramedic. Because it feels like my passion is slowly just being ripped out of me. What I fought for so long to become has irrelevant so I regret it fully, whole heartedly. Waste of my time

Lesiba: i will not trivialize and downplay the anxiety, the concern and the people's fears because its unknown ground, unknown territory we're entering

VO: For those that are already in the system, they’re hoping that there can be an inclusive solution for everyone.

Willie: its as if the educational system say we never existed

Tegan: They haven't even indicated to us that there will be a way for us to bridge across, we have the hours on the road, if we could bridge across into the degrees that would be affordable for a lot of us to actually go and be able to do it

In 80% of emergencies, patients rely on the care of basic life support practitioners, who have generally qualified through 4-week short courses, which government says are not up to the professional standards required. But new regulations will signal the end of short courses and EMS practitioners will be forced to complete formal degrees of up to 4 years. This has sparked fears that it will result in an even bigger shortage of advanced life-support practitioners. Carte Blanche investigates Script: Dispatch: Private Ambulance services do you have an emergency?…. My wife has been shot. She is dying please VO: Violent Crimes and High accident road deaths make South Africa one of the most perilous countries in the world. With over 14000 road fatalities reported in 2016, we often rely on emergency care givers to be our life savers. Tegan: if I don't get up in the morning and come to work and help someone that person is going to die so the reason I do it is to [00:08:19.10] give someone an extra day VO: Tegan Genlloud is one of the many dedicated emergency care givers with over 6 years experience. Dispatch: The Ambulance is 3 minutes away. Is your wife still breathing? LINK: On the HPCSA register there are around, 55 000 emergency care personnel with only a 4 week basic life support qualification. Around 18 000 of them are employed by industry while the rest are unemployed or worse, under skilled. So are we really receiving the best care there is? Beat// person screaming on side of the stretcher VO: This privately filmed footage by an emergency care giver was sent to Carte Blanche. At this accident scene two basic life support medics are attending to some of the injured. We can clearly see that they have omitted to treat a severely injured person, then proceed to load him into the ambulance through the side door - dropping the patient in the process. This kind of malpractice is not uncommon according to John, a highly experienced advanced life support paramedic. His identity is protected for fear of being targeted by other industry players. Jon: The quality in all honesty is shocking. They have a certificate that says that they are competent in various skills, yet when they come to work they are unable to perform any of those basic skills. They won't even know if a patient has a pulse or doesn't have a pulse. VO: At this accident scene - Basic life support crews are clearly violating the medical code of ethics, loading 10 injured patients into one Ambulance, then making some of them sit on the front seat without even treating them. John: there are lot of these small little fringe private services popping up, but there is no proper regulation. They don't have the basic equipment that's needed for the patient. . They will put 11 or 12 patients in an ambulance to go and claim against the road accident fund. LINK: Rogue elements appear to have emerged within the emergency medical services industry, tarnishing the profession. In addition dishonest private colleges have mushroomed around the country offering short courses, churning out Basic Ambulance assistants by the thousands. John: People have these high hopes they can go and do a four week course, pay anything from 8 to 15,16 thousand rand for their four week course, they do the course, thinking they're going to be a paramedic but they're not a paramedic they're a medic. And now that they have this qualification they believe they can get employment and it doesn't happen. VO: After qualifying, desperate basic ambulance assistants can find themselves jobless and penniless, Zodwa Sibanyoni is one such victim Zodwa:I quit my job to go and study to be a paramedic as it was a passion of mine. VO: She qualified 3 years ago as a Basic Ambulance Assistant and paid R11 500 for her course. Zodwa: They just tell you that it is a jungle out there. They don’t tell you that there a lot of you out there and you might not get a job. Zodwa: I tend to suffer from depression at times My health has deteriorated as a result VO: Although there are many credible institutions producing competent medics, John knows of some that are unscrupulous. John: There was some college in Limpopo where some people were coming on a Friday and on Saturday would fetch their certificate and then when they're employed what happens is, they cant even take a blood pressure LINK: In January this year the department of health introduced a new regulation that no longer recognizes the short course training for all emergency medical services. VO: Lesiba Malotana of the HPCSA says the short courses do not help to professionalise the emergency care industry, especially with so many jobless. Lesiba : Thats correct they're no longer going to produce more and the rationale is that there is enough. and if they’re not able to find employment is there a need to continue producing? Is that not perpetrating unemployment even poverty Zodwa: The government posts are only advertised once a year. I haven’t even seen any in a while. I keep applying but nothing happens. 75% of the people I went to class with we’re all unemployed. Lesiba: the short courses are just skills based while if you want to produce a competent wholesome practitioner. why should an entry level paramedic not end up with a PhD in emergency care VO: By the end of this year the 4 week Basic life support course will be discontinued and replaced with a full time one year Higher certificate. The 4 month Intermediate course will be stopped by 2019, replaced with a 2 year diploma and the 9 month Advance Life support course also ends by 2019, replaced with a 4 year degree. VO: Willie Lightfoot an ambulance service provider and veteran paramedic, says these changes are going to lead to a crisis. Willie: its not going to be enough personnel that can man the ambulance, especially on advanced life support. VO: Advanced life Support practitioners are already in short supply, they're a scarce skill and easily poached internationally. Willie: the one big problem that we see is the ICU transfers, in other words the guys that really are critical, babies that are choking, people that stopped breathing, there is not going to be enough advanced life support paramedics, because it now takes 4 years to get an advanced qualified paramedics on the new system VO: Tegan is an intermediate life support medic, and has first hand experience on how a shortage of advanced life support paramedics plays out in an emergency situation. Tegan: they will dispatch an ambulance out first and then the ambulance will assess the situation and if we need further equipment or drugs or anything that is in the advanced scope of practice we will phone for that vehicle to come out and assist us the likelihood of getting a paramedic on one of the ambulances is minimal John: if there are 70 life support paramedics in Gauteng and you are sending 50 of them on a 4 year course, where are you going to get the other 50 to replace them? VO: At present there are only 4 universities offering the four year degree, and a fifth one coming on board soon. They will produce about 60 to 100 B-Tech graduates per year, who will eventually replace the current Advanced Life Support paramedics but that won't be enough to feed into the system, says Christiaan Visser, from the emergency medical care training association. Christiaan: Nobody is fighting against upgrading the short courses, nobody is saying that we shouldn't have tertiary education,. What we are saying is who's going to fill up the gap between short course trained people and tertiary education. If you look at the staff turn over in the ambulance industry it is much higher than that amount that the universities are able to produce VO: It also means that current medics who want to advance their short course qualification will have to go into full time study. Tegan has already spent 94 000 rand on her courses and is still paying back the debt Tegan: for me there is no way forward with my expenses I cant take 2 years off of work or 4 years off of work and go and study that higher qualification, John: The problem is would your company pay for you to take 5 years off work or 4 years off work to go and study full time at university and they employ another paramedic in your place so they're paying dual salary...My company won't do that Willie: they would rather downgrade the current critical care paramedics like us to a lower level so we cant do the skill, so we did it yesterday if they change the law I cant help you with my medicine, I cant give it anymore Link: The HPCSA is the body that sets the scope for the curriculum for all emergency medical care staff. They admit that the curriculum is below par. Lesiba : i think one of the biggest things we must never do is pretend these people have not been the backbone of health system Unfortunately, the difficulties is when the course was so badly designed that is cant be repackaged to be able to articulate into something LINK: Discussions have been going on since 2003 to upgrade the qualification but stakeholders say that the voice of the industry is falling on deaf ears Christiaan: We've written many letters to the health profession council asking do you understand the implication of closing the short courses, do you understand whats going to happen to the industry and the public? John: We know nothing, we haven't received any information - everything is done behind closed doors and we only know through it leaking out .In 15 years i've had one newsletter posted to me VO: As part of the fallout many of the colleges offering short courses will have to close down. Accreditation is a long and costly process. Christiaan: At the moment there are around 30 private education and training providers who will have to close their doors so we're looking at 2000 job losses John: I personally am all for them stopping the basic ambulance courses, it's a quick money making scheme that even four weeks you're turning over millions and there's been no proper regulation Zodwa: I regret doing the course, I regret being a paramedic. Because it feels like my passion is slowly just being ripped out of me. What I fought for so long to become has irrelevant so I regret it fully, whole heartedly. Waste of my time Lesiba: i will not trivialize and downplay the anxiety, the concern and the people's fears because its unknown ground, unknown territory we're entering VO: For those that are already in the system, they’re hoping that there can be an inclusive solution for everyone. Willie: its as if the educational system say we never existed Tegan: They haven't even indicated to us that there will be a way for us to bridge across, we have the hours on the road, if we could bridge across into the degrees that would be affordable for a lot of us to actually go and be able to do it

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): When you dial 10111 in a medical emergency you rely on proficient care on the spot. New regulation on EMS personnel qualifications threatens to put your life, and their livelihoods on the line.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In January 2017 the Health Professionals council of South Africa and the Department of health introduced a new regulation that revokes recognition of the six-week basic life support, six-month intermediate life support and nine-month advanced life support courses for paramedics, that have been serving the industry up till now. A basic life support paramedic now has to complete a two-year course, and those wanting to become advanced life support paramedics must do a four-year degree. This could put the entire industry in jeopardy as well as put our live's in danger.
metadata.Summary: The new regulation has evoked concern amongst EMS practitioners and private Emergency service providers as well as private training academies, that it will limit progress for individuals already in the system with six weeks basic or even intermediary life support qualifications, as this means that in order to now get higher qualifications they would quit their jobs in order to attend a mandatory full time course for three years or more to get more qualified in the field. Paul Masita, a 50 year old Intermediary Paramedic fears his career advancement is over, he has a family and two children to support and full time study would be out of the question. The colleges currently running the short courses will have to close those programmes down and there is no light coming for accreditation from the HPCSA and SAQA. With only four universities currently running with the courses how are we going to get enough paramedic's into the field? The Department of Health is adamant that they want to professionalise the industry even if there is some collateral damage along the way. They assert that many of these colleges are cash cows, churning out basic paramedic's who may never find a job. In the mean time we may not have services that can effectively save lives or even worse they could end up costing the average citizen a lot more. Paramedic's with degrees are far more expensive to hire. A group of concerned Emergency Services providers and organizations are not taking this lying down and are planning on taking the Department of Health to court later this month. Carte Blanche investigates.
metadata.Further information: There are about 140 000 registered basic life support paramedics on the HPCSA register and only about 18 thousand of them are employed. South Africa already has a shortage of intermediate and advance life support paramedics, even with the current system of short courses qualifications. In 2008 South Africa had 1631 registered advanced life support (ALS) paramedics to provide pre-hospital advanced life support care to a population of approximately 50 million. Compared to globally accepted ratios, the number of ALS paramedics in South Africa can be considered as grossly inadequate. The reasoning behind this regulation is that is that the profession needs to be recognized within the current educational framework and the current short courses do not provide that. The regulation will also eliminate bogus colleges that have used the system as a cash cow while producing unskilled paramedics into the system. However the short courses academies has been a reliable system for the health industry until now producing over 60 basic life support paramedics every 6 weeks who would then work their way to becoming Advance life support practitioners within a short time of two to three years. From 2018 onwards the HPCSA will effectively close its register only recognizing a university qualification from a two-year basic life support course to a four-year Advance life support qualification. There are currently only four universities offering the course, being the University of Johannesburg, University of the western cape, Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University and the Durban University of technology. According to Oliver Wright, CEO of South African Ambulance emergency services association, besides the fact that university education is inaccessible and expensive for many South Africans with poor financial background, the course will now only be offered in four provinces making it hard for ordinary citizens to acquire the qualification. The Paramedics industry is also hard hit by an exodus of skilled professionals leaving the country every year to work in countries where they get paid over R100 000 tax free monthly as compared to the 20 to 30 000 they would get here as advanced life support medics. To add to that there is also professionals that retire every year, so with all that, it will be very difficult to replace these skilled workers with only four universities producing about 60 graduates annually that have very little practical experience. Christiaan, a director at the De Vries academy in Pretoria one of the largest EMS academies in the country also made mention that with the fact that they will now be required to shut down their operations, this adds to the long queue of unemployment for many people across the country which in recent weeks has been said to be at it’s most highest since 2003. Cris says the De Vries academy and other associations are currently in the process of taking the Department of Health to the court of law to have this new regulation reviewed. They hope for the filing process complete by June. Generally it is believed that the regulation is good for the EMS industry but the concern is the fact that the government is quick to shut down the short courses without outlining a clear plan to curb the low number of Intermediate and Advance life support professionals that are to be produced by the University. The government sector is already the hardest hit in this shortage compared to the private sector and it is a national problem primarily in rural arrears of the country. Does this mean that dying South Africans might soon be in trouble due to a lack of enough skilled professionals on at an emergency scene? Carte Blanche investigates. We speak first to Neil Gargan, chairman of South African Ambulance emergency services association as he shares with us his concerns. Oliver will also highlight the shocking statistics of how many qualified paramedics are employed in the country as well and his view in terms of where he feels the shortage will come from as well as his journey with the HPCSA and the Department of health when he tried to address his concern with them. Case study- Paul Masita is a 50-year-old paramedic who has been on the job for over 15 years. He has an Intermediate life support qualification acquired through the short courses. Paul is a family man and is hoping to study further to get a an Advanced life support qualification but with the new regulation he fears he can’t achieve that as he does not have the luxury to quit his job and go to university full time. Chris, Manager at De Vries academy tells us how long their academy has been running from and how many skilled paramedics have they produced. He also shares with us how shutting their academy doors will affect them both from a point of employment as well practitioners in the Emergency services. Along with other academies and associations, they plan to take The Department of Health and the HPCSA to court before end of June 2017. David Stanton from NetCare 911 sees the regulation as a good thing and something that will have the industry in a good place in the next 20 years. According to Dave this is not something that’s unique to South Africa but he does agree that there might be a learning gap created that the government hasn’t really addressed as far as the paramedics in the current system are concerned. Case Study- Tegan Gudlloud is a 26-year-old passionate paramedic. She has an intermediate Life support qualification that has already cost her over R90000 in fees. She has a desire to study further and become and Advanced life support paramedic. Tegan’s challenge now is that if she is to study further she will have to quit her job and attend varsity full time. She feels this will put her under financial strain and that quitting her job is not an option that will suit her. Mr Raveen Naidoo, Director of EMS at the NDH says the regulation will work. When is it supposed to take effect? According to him there is a plan to curb the anticipated further decline in the number of graduates produced annually. Raveen believes the new regulation has been in the pipeline for a while and that the private training academies knew about it and their concerns are only from a commercial point of view. Willie Lightfoot is the CEO of LifeMed Private Ambulance services. Willie says the new regulation will hamper them as business people because they will not be willing to pay someone for the duration of them attending a full time cause. The financial implications of having to pay higher salaries to the university qualified people who will be doing the same jobs as the short current ones is also a an issue Willie is opposed to. HPCSA, on the regulation and how they think it will impact the industry and what measures are they putting in place to fill the gap when there is a shortage of EMS professionals in the field, and what are they going to do to ensure that the current paramedics' advancement is not hampered by this new regulation. How are they going to ensure that the public is not jeopardised when critical medical care is in short supply? Ultimately the Government’s regulation is believed to be a good initiative in the long run, however the impact that it will have on the many paramedics and the private businesses in the industry seems to be an oversight on their part. How this new regulation affect the normal south African in the streets in times of emergency in the future and will the industry itself take a knock as private ambulance agencies are forced to shutdown? Carte Blanche investigates.
